content: Bronchiolitis is an acute inflammatory condition affecting the bronchioles, predominantly seen in infants and young children. It is most commonly caused by the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). The management of bronchiolitis varies significantly among clinicians, largely due to the absence of robust evidence supporting a specific treatment strategy. The leukotriene pathway has been implicated in the pathogenesis of bronchiolitis, and leukotriene inhibitors, such as montelukast, have been utilized in this population. However, the findings from the limited number of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) conducted to date are inconsistent, necessitating a comprehensive evaluation of their efficacy and safety in treating bronchiolitis in infants and young children. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of leukotriene inhibitors in the treatment of bronchiolitis in infants and young children. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, LILACS, Web of Science, WHO ICTRP, and ClinicalTrials.gov, up to May 2014. The inclusion criteria were RCTs comparing leukotriene inhibitors with placebo or other interventions in children under two years of age diagnosed with bronchiolitis. The primary outcomes assessed were the length of hospital stay and all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included clinical severity scores, percentage of symptom-free days, percentage of children requiring ventilation, oxygen saturation, recurrent wheezing, respiratory rate, and adverse effects. Five studies, involving a total of 1,296 participants under two years of age hospitalized with bronchiolitis, were included in the review. Two studies, assessed as having a low risk of bias, compared the daily administration of 4 mg montelukast (a leukotriene inhibitor) from admission until discharge with a placebo. These studies evaluated the length of hospital stay as the primary outcome and clinical severity scores as a secondary outcome. However, the effects of leukotriene inhibitors on these outcomes were uncertain due to significant heterogeneity between the study results and wide confidence intervals. Specifically, the mean difference (MD) in hospital stay was -0.95 days (95% confidence interval [CI]: -3.08 to 1.19, P = 0.38), and the clinical severity score on day two showed an MD of -0.57 (95% CI: -2.37 to 1.23, P = 0.53). On day three, the clinical severity score had an MD of 0.17 (95% CI: -1.93 to 2.28, P = 0.87). The quality of evidence for these outcomes was rated as low. The remaining three studies investigated the use of montelukast over several weeks to prevent post-bronchiolitis symptoms, comparing it with placebo. One of these studies was assessed as having a low risk of bias, while the other two were deemed to have a high risk of attrition bias. Due to substantial clinical heterogeneity in disease severity, treatment duration, outcome measures, and timing of assessments, the results of these studies were not pooled. Individual analyses did not demonstrate significant differences between the leukotriene inhibitor group and the control group in terms of symptom-free days or the incidence of recurrent wheezing. One study, involving 952 children, reported two deaths in the leukotriene inhibitor group, but neither death was attributed to the drug. No data were available regarding the percentage of children requiring ventilation, oxygen saturation, or respiratory rate. Adverse events were reported in three studies and included diarrhea, wheezing shortly after administration, and rash. No significant differences in adverse events were observed between the leukotriene inhibitor and control groups. In conclusion, the current evidence does not provide definitive support for the use of leukotriene inhibitors in reducing the length of hospital stay or improving clinical severity scores in infants and young children with bronchiolitis. The quality of the evidence was rated as low due to unexplained high levels of statistical heterogeneity and imprecision resulting from small sample sizes and wide confidence intervals, which did not exclude the possibility of no effect or harm. Data on symptom-free days and recurrent wheezing were derived from single studies only, limiting their generalizability. Further large-scale studies are required to clarify the role of leukotriene inhibitors in this population. One ongoing registered study may contribute to future updates of this review.
